analysis.one_liner: Lets student loan borrowers wipe out their student debt in bankruptcy like other debt.
analysis.headline: The bill to make student loans dischargeable in bankruptcy never left committee; it died with only 2 cosponsors and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, student loans are one of the few debts you generally cannot erase in bankruptcy — credit card debt, medical bills, and business loans can all be discharged, but student loans usually follow you for life unless you prove 'undue hardship.' This bill would strike that exception, letting borrowers discharge federal, private, and nonprofit student loans in bankruptcy, along with obligations to repay scholarships or stipends. The change would apply only to loans taken out after the bill became law. It never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Future borrowers whose debts turn out to be unpayable — people who lose their jobs, face medical crises, or were sold degrees that did not pay off — would be able to start over rather than carry the debt indefinitely. Borrowers would also gain negotiating leverage with lenders, since the threat of discharge could push lenders to work out reduced settlements.

how_it_helps.text: The bill strikes the student-loan exception in the bankruptcy code, so student loans — government, nonprofit, or private — would be dischargeable like other unsecured debt.
It would also let borrowers discharge obligations to repay educational benefits, scholarships, or stipends.

analysis.who_pays: Lenders and holders of student loans — private lenders, nonprofits that lend to students, and the federal government's loan program — would absorb more losses when borrowers file for bankruptcy, and would likely price that risk into interest rates for future borrowers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Student loan lenders and the federal loan program

drawbacks.text: Making loans dischargeable raises lenders' expected losses, so interest rates on student loans would likely rise and some lenders might tighten credit, making borrowing more expensive or harder for weaker applicants.
The change applies only to debts arising after enactment, so borrowers already drowning in existing loans would get no relief from this bill.

Critics of broad dischargeability argue that easy bankruptcy forgiveness could encourage some borrowers to walk away from debts the taxpayer-backed system financed, shifting costs back to the federal loan program.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real: bankruptcy exists precisely so that people crushed by unpayable debts can restart, and student loans are the one major debt carved out of that protection. The main cost is higher borrowing costs as lenders price in the new risk, and the bill offers nothing to the millions already holding student debt. Those costs are honest tradeoffs of the policy, not reasons the bill was flawed in design — but its two-cosponsor support and instant death in committee meant the tradeoff was never seriously weighed by Congress.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to a subcommittee, got no hearing or markup, and expired when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Glenn Grothman introduced the bill on February 13, 2020, with Reps. Lou Correa and Ralph Norman as the only cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, then referred to the Subcommittee on Antitrust, Commercial, and Administrative Law on March 10, 2020.
No further action was recorded before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Student loan lenders and the federal loan program keep the status quo: student debts generally cannot be erased in bankruptcy, so borrowers with unpayable loans keep paying. Nobody who supported the bill got a hearing on it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Lenders who keep the bankruptcy exception

industries.note: These lenders depend on the bankruptcy exception: once a borrower signs, the debt generally follows them for life, which is why defaults can be pursued for decades. Dischargeability would let distressed borrowers wipe out these loans, raising lender losses. Their interest in keeping the exception runs directly against borrowers who need relief.

The federal government holds most student debt and, under the exception, can collect on defaults for decades, garnish wages, and offset benefits. Dischargeability would increase federal losses on defaulted loans, though the same exception is what traps borrowers.

industries.industry: Student loan debt collectors and servicers
industries.note: Servicers and collectors earn fees on accounts kept in repayment, including on old defaulted debt. More discharges would shrink the stock of collectible debt they administer.
The bill explicitly covers loans from nonprofits and states, which currently enjoy the same protection from borrower bankruptcy that private lenders have.
